newsitem.title: USA: CSCE cocoa ends thinly traded session firmer.
newsitem.headline: CSCE cocoa ends thinly traded session firmer.

text.p: CSCE cocoa futures ended a bit higher in lackluster trading Wednesday, lifted by a late-session round of local short-covering, dealers said.
With closing volume only reaching an estimated 3,471 lots and prices confined to a narrow range, traders lamented the waning interest in cocoa futures.
"The market has gone into a holiday mode already," one trader said. "There is a lack of new business."
He said the most-active March contract appeared to be stuck in a near-term range between $1,373 and $1,400 a tonne.

March futures ended at $1,389, up $5, having traded from $1,390 to $1,378. May rose $2, to $1,409. Spot December finished down $6, to $1,327. With two days to go before December's expiry, open interest on the contract was only six lots.
The market sagged in early going pressured by trade selling, dealers said, but manufacturer interest toward the lows stemmed losses and forced locals to cover their short positions, traders said.
Technically, traders continued to see the $1,373-1,372 level as strong support. Nearby resistance was pegged at $1,395, with the $1,400 seen as a key psychological hurdle.

There was little reaction to the latest Ivorian arrival figures. Ivorian exporters and traders pegged the total arrivals by December 7 at between 330,000 and 350,000 tonnes, down from an estimated 410,000 tonnes the same time last year.
"It just serves as a confirmation that arrivals are lower than last year -- as expected," the trader said.

He added that a forecast by a senior Ivorian diplomat, who said 1996/97 cocoa output was likely to be between 850,000 and 900,000 tonnes, was bullish because it could point to a world cocoa deficit of about 300,000 tonnes.
Forecasts for a world cocoa deficit in 1996/97 season have ranged widely from 20,000 to 259,000 tonnes.
